builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?
summary: sudo L7 replaces ad hoc or test-pass-only evaluation of coding agents with 60 staff-engineer-authored tasks graded against 1,287 hidden atomic rubric criteria spanning eight behavioral dimensions, including truthful reporting and risk flagging. Adopting it costs nothing in infrastructure since results are on a public leaderboard, but replicating the grading methodology internally requires an agentic grader that reads transcripts, runs code, and treats test output as evidence, which adds evaluation pipeline complexity. It can fail as a selection tool because tasks are built around prior frontier-model failures in mostly private codebases, so scores may not transfer to the reader's domain, and model grader agreement with humans is only 85-86%, leaving roughly one in seven criterion verdicts unreliable.
rationale: The paper is an evaluation benchmark, so its actionable value for a constrained team is using the public leaderboard and the rubric methodology to select coding-agent models and to audit agent transcripts before production reliance.
technique: Rubric-based behavioral benchmark for coding agents

claims.statement: sudo L7 replaces ad hoc or test-pass-only evaluation of coding agents with 60 staff-engineer-authored tasks graded against 1,287 hidden atomic rubric criteria spanning eight behavioral dimensions, including truthful reporting and risk flagging. Adopting it costs nothing in infrastructure since results are on a public leaderboard, but replicating the grading methodology internally requires an agentic grader that reads transcripts, runs code, and treats test output as evidence, which adds evaluation pipeline complexity. It can fail as a selection tool because tasks are built around prior frontier-model failures in mostly private codebases, so scores may not transfer to the reader's domain, and model grader agreement with humans is only 85-86%, leaving roughly one in seven criterion verdicts unreliable.

Leaderboard results, not a technique improvement: Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6%, Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%, mid-tier models 31-34%, and 13 other models at most 18.9%; model graders agreed with a human engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts.
